doc.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021

title: Early listening: TV jazz scores, 45s and Lou Stein's 'Soft Sands'
summary: He first heard jazz in late-1950s TV cop-show scores; his parents had only 45s, including Lou Stein's 'Soft Sands', which he later requested from Stein on a club date.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Okay. Was there something, I read an anecdote about you hearing the Ellington band and how much an impression — I’m also wondering if there was something in your household, LPs or radio or something that helped set you on your eventual path?
Well do you want me to tell the story about the Ellington band etcetera, etcetera? Shall I start there?

Well yeah, I’m more curious because I’ve been interested in how every generation has their high tech things that their entertainment is delivered through. And when we think back to, you and I are close in age and if we think back to our formative years, the high tech at that time, so what was in your household that you might have heard music from?

Well I mean aside from television, in the late 50s if you recall there was a sudden surge of jazz oriented scores for TV cop shows, like “Peter Gunn,” “Mr. Lucky,” “Johnny Staccato,” “Checkmates,” all these forgotten TV shows that people like Henry Mancini and John Williams and Pete Rugolo and Johnny Mandel and others were writing scores for. So I heard this music, beginning with “Peter Gunn” when I was about five years old and this was some of the first music I can remember hearing and some of the first jazz I can remember hearing. And it all just hit me remarkably hard. Just the harmony, all these hip harmonies, and the rhythms of course, and of course all these scores were played by some of the hippest jazz musicians in LA at the time. So that was a big exposure to jazz and to music, and also my parents were very low tech. I mean they didn’t even have LPs until I got seriously interested in music and they finally bought a stereo, you know, to play LPs. But for much of my childhood all we had was the 45 RPM record player to play. So they had a handful of 45s, Glenn Miller things, Tex Beneke, you know. Actually there was a, do you remember a piano player named Lou Stein? © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

He was a really good jazz piano player who was active in the 40s, 50s, until maybe twenty years ago, active in New York, played with a lot of people. And one of the 45s that my mother had was the thing that Lou had, it was kind of a fluke hit called “Soft Sands.” And so I remember playing that a lot of times and I memorized the melody and could play it on my horns, on clarinet to begin with. So fast forward, oh God, ‘til the late 1980s and I end up on this club date, by club date I’m using the musician’s term, you know weddings, bar mitzvahs, private parties, that sort. So I ended up on a club date in Connecticut with Lou Stein. So we were in the middle of this gig and we’re just playing dinner music or something. And I said, “Could we play ‘Soft Sands’?” I thought his jaw was going to hit the floor you know. It was great fun. So we played “Soft Sands.” You know I’m sure he’d never gotten a request for that in his life.
